component.name: Apache Fineract
component.description: Multi-tenant core banking platform exposing REST APIs for back-office users (loan officers, tellers, administrators) to manage clients, loans, savings, deposits, and accounting. Runs as an executable JAR or container behind a reverse proxy or WAF, with Spring Batch close-of-business jobs and external business events published to Kafka or ActiveMQ. Fineract provides an API only (no web UI) and is not designed to be embedded as a library.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it.

blueprints.name: Fineract deployment
blueprints.description: Deployment described by the Fineract threat model: untrusted internet traffic reaches a reverse proxy or WAF over TLS, which forwards to the Fineract API server (embedded Tomcat); the application talks to a PostgreSQL or MariaDB database over an authenticated, per-tenant JDBC connection pool with schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant isolation. The API surface is the primary trust boundary; the filesystem and the database connection pool are secondary boundaries where data is treated as trusted.

assets.name: Fineract API server
assets.description: Embedded Tomcat serving the REST API. Tenant resolution happens at request entry via the Fineract-Platform-TenantId header; once a request has passed authentication and tenant resolution, data inside the application is treated as trusted.

assets.name: Reverse proxy / WAF
assets.description: Operator-provided NGINX or cloud-native load balancer terminating TLS and providing rate limiting, IP filtering, and DDoS mitigation. The project explicitly recommends never running Fineract directly on the internet.

assets.name: Database (PostgreSQL or MariaDB)
assets.description: Tenant data schemas reached over JDBC with credentials from application.properties or environment variables; SQL generated by the application is trusted by the database.

assets.name: Filesystem
assets.description: Secondary trust boundary: the application assumes all disk read and write operations are safe.

zones.name: Untrusted internet
zones.description: Network-based attackers and remote API clients before authentication.

zones.name: Perimeter
zones.description: Reverse proxy, WAF, or API gateway terminating TLS in front of Fineract.

zones.name: Fineract application
zones.description: The API server process; data is trusted after authentication and tenant resolution.

zones.name: Data layer
zones.description: Database and filesystem; trusted by the application.

persona.description: Sysadmin with root access who configures and deploys the application. Trusted.
Loan officers, branch managers, and system admins holding tenant-scoped credentials; authenticated and authorized through RBAC.
Direct access from bank customers to Fineract is out of model; the self-service plugin is a separate repository (openMF/selfservice-plugin), as is the Community App web UI (openMF/web-app).

assumptions.description: Runs on any OS with a compatible JVM (Azul Zulu recommended); PostgreSQL is the recommended database. The JVM, OS, database, and dependency supply chain are assumed uncompromised.
Multi-tenancy is implemented via schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant, with tenant resolution at request entry from the Fineract-Platform-TenantId header.

The JVM system clock is trusted for business-date logic, close-of-business scheduling, and audit timestamps; clock manipulation causing incorrect interest accrual or batch behavior is an environmental issue, not a Fineract bug.

A reverse proxy, WAF, or API gateway sits in front of Fineract in production, enforcing TLS with a CA-trusted certificate, rate limiting, and request size limits; side channels (timing and cache attacks) are not modeled.

threats.name: Network attacker gains authentication or extracts data via injection
threats.description: An unauthenticated network-based attacker who can send HTTP requests to the API attempts to gain authentication or extract data via injection. The attacker can observe TLS-encrypted traffic but not decrypt it without certificate compromise.

threats.name: Cross-tenant data access
threats.description: An authenticated back-office user with valid credentials for one tenant accesses users or data of another tenant. Tenant isolation is a claimed security property: users and data of tenant A must be inaccessible from tenant B.

threats.name: Privilege escalation by a low-privilege back-office user
threats.description: An authenticated low-privilege user (for example a loan officer) escalates privileges, performs admin actions, or modifies loans and disbursements they do not own. RBAC enforcement is a claimed security property.

threats.name: Denial of service via resource exhaustion
threats.description: Fineract does not provide rate limiting or brute-force protection; the embedded Tomcat has configurable connection limits, but volumetric DDoS mitigation is explicitly left to the reverse proxy or cloud provider. Request size limits should also be enforced at the proxy.

threats.name: Arbitrary SQL through admin custom reports
threats.description: Fineract allows administrators to define custom reports with SQL; an attacker who gains admin access can execute arbitrary SQL through the reporting module. This is by design (an admin capability) and not a vulnerability.

threats.name: Tampering with audit logs
threats.description: Audit logs are written to the database and filesystem with no append-only or cryptographic integrity guarantee; audit log tamper-resistance is a property the project explicitly does not provide.

threats.name: MITM via the embedded self-signed keystore
threats.description: Using the embedded SSL keystore in production is a known misuse pattern: keystore.jks is self-signed and its private key is public (shipped in the JAR), leaving users vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. Exposing the API directly to the internet without a reverse proxy is likewise misuse: the embedded Tomcat is not hardened for direct exposure and there is no built-in rate limiting.

threats.name: Physical or OS-level access to the database or application host
threats.description: If an attacker has OS-level access to the PostgreSQL/MariaDB host or root on the Fineract host, the model assumes the game is already lost; this adversary is explicitly out of scope, as are compromised reverse proxies (infrastructure-layer) and supply-chain compromise of the JVM, OS, database, or dependencies. Encryption at rest is not provided by Fineract and must be done at the storage layer.

threats.name: System clock manipulation
threats.description: Fineract relies on the JVM system clock for business-date logic, close-of-business scheduling, and audit timestamps; if the clock is manipulated, loan interest accrual and COB batch behavior may be incorrect. Treated as an environmental issue, not a Fineract bug.

trustBoundaries.name: Internet perimeter boundary
trustBoundaries.description: TLS-encrypted traffic from the untrusted internet reaches the reverse proxy; certificate validation is required. The project ships a self-signed certificate for localhost only; production requires a CA-trusted certificate or a managed proxy.

trustBoundaries.name: API surface trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The primary trust boundary. Once a request has passed authentication and tenant resolution (via the Fineract-Platform-TenantId header), data inside the application is treated as trusted. X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto are respected when a proxy is present.

trustBoundaries.name: Data layer trust boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Secondary trust boundaries: the database trusts SQL generated by the application (JDBC over an authenticated per-tenant connection pool), and the application assumes all filesystem operations are safe.

controls.name: Tenant isolation
controls.description: Users and data of tenant A are inaccessible from tenant B, via schema-per-tenant or database-per-tenant separation and per-tenant authenticated connection pools.

controls.name: Role-based access control enforcement
controls.description: RBAC enforcement so low-privilege users cannot perform admin actions.

controls.name: Password strength enforcement
controls.description: Password strength enforcement for back-office user credentials.

controls.name: HTTPS encryption
controls.description: HTTPS encryption for the API, with an operator-provided valid certificate.

controls.name: Enable OAuth2 with an external identity provider
controls.description: Enable and configure OAuth2 instead of Basic Auth, using a separate trusted identity provider such as Keycloak (external identity provider support is built in).

controls.name: Enable two-factor authentication
controls.description: Enable 2FA (FINERACT_SECURITY_2FA_ENABLED=true) and configure a secure SMS or email gateway for production admin accounts.

controls.name: Deploy behind a reverse proxy / WAF / API gateway
controls.description: Deploy a reverse proxy, WAF, or API gateway in front of Fineract to enforce rate limiting, IP filtering, DDoS mitigation, and request size limits; the project explicitly recommends not running directly on the internet.

controls.name: Replace the embedded SSL keystore
controls.description: Replace the embedded self-signed keystore with a CA-trusted certificate, or terminate TLS at the reverse proxy, before exposing the service to any network.

controls.name: Run database migrations separately
controls.description: Run Liquibase database migrations separately from the application server in production, or ensure the app server's migration-only privileges are dropped after startup.

controls.name: Segregate instance types
controls.description: In large deployments run batch managers and workers on separate nodes from API-serving nodes, and use read-only instances for reporting.

controls.name: Encrypt data at rest at the storage layer
controls.description: Fineract does not provide encryption at rest; the operator must encrypt data at rest at the storage layer.
